sections.title: A practical home for your next app

blocks.text: SoftN brings an editable interface, application logic and local data together in a portable app. You can shape an app visually in Builder, use your own AI provider in Studio, or work directly with its source. Runtime opens the result so you can use it.

These guides follow the decisions you actually make: what to build, which tool to open, how to change the app, where its records live, and how to share it. You do not need to understand a virtual machine before changing a heading.

sections.title: Understand the pieces as you need them

blocks.text: A .ui file describes the interface. JavaScript-compatible .logic supplies behaviour through the ZIPP engine. XDB supplies app-scoped records. The host is the browser, desktop application or hosting platform that runs the app and decides which capabilities it may use.

A .softn bundle carries editable client material. A private backend is a separate deployment concern. Keeping that distinction clear makes exports easier to understand and helps avoid shipping private server material by accident.

The guides explain the documented public workflow and include small examples. They are not an exhaustive specification of every component property. Follow the source links at the end of a page for the underlying project reference, and check the host you plan to deploy before relying on an optional capability.

Feature descriptions were reviewed against the accessible project documentation on 15 September 2026. Python and advanced host integrations have their own boundaries. Examples in this edition have been checked against the documented syntax, not executed inside a SoftN runtime during preparation.

pages.summary: An introduction to the editable app format, the tools around it, and the choices you keep after building an app.

seo.title: What is SoftN? | SoftN Docs
seo.description: What is SoftN? Understand its open-source app platform, portable .softn files, visual tools, JavaScript logic and browser or desktop hosts.

sections.title: One app you can open, edit and run

blocks.text: SoftN is an open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable apps on the web and desktop. Its portable .softn format packages the interface, client logic, data seeds and assets so an app can be reopened and changed rather than treated as a finished black box.

That gives you several ways to start. Explore an existing app, change a project in Builder, describe an idea in Studio using a configured AI provider, or write the source yourself. These are different routes into the same editable app, not separate product formats.

items.description: The workspace for visual editing, source editing, data modelling and previewing an app.
The AI-assisted creation workflow. Configure a provider, describe the app and review what it generates.
The host-facing app experience for opening and running bundles, including a browser library and desktop options.
The ZIP-based app bundle you can export, share, reopen and customise.

blocks.text: You do not need an AI account to open the Fieldnotes example or edit source manually. AI-assisted generation is an optional creation path.

sections.title: From useful forms to interactive experiences

blocks.text: The built-in component library covers layouts, forms, data displays, charts and dashboards. Audio, animation and Three.js scenes extend the format to games and richer interactive apps, subject to the relevant host support and permissions.

A small planner is a good first app because it exercises input, logic, records and presentation without adding external services. A connected business dashboard adds another layer: authenticated backend actions, a server database and an access policy.

sections.title: Portable does not mean every host is identical

blocks.text: The bundle transports the editable client. It does not automatically transport a running backend, external credentials, another user’s records or permission grants. A browser host and a desktop host can expose different capabilities.

blocks.title: Keep ownership practical
blocks.text: Keep an exported bundle or source-controlled project you can restore. Local browser storage is useful working storage, but it should not be your only copy of something important.

SoftN, ZIPP and XDB have different responsibilities. SoftN renders the app and connects its parts; ZIPP executes client logic; XDB provides local records. FormLogic is an optional hosted integration, not a prerequisite for a standalone app.

Open Fieldnotes, change a heading in Builder, preview the result and export it. Reopen the export in Runtime. That short loop introduces the central promise of the format: the thing you run remains something you can edit.

sections.title: Begin with something that already works

blocks.text: Fieldnotes is the repository’s introductory task planner. Its interface, .logic and XDB records demonstrate one complete app. Start there rather than inventing a bundle manifest before you have seen the editing workflow.

items.title: Open Fieldnotes in Builder
items.text: Use the homepage’s example action. Identify the preview, the selected component’s properties and the source view.

items.title: Change the heading
items.text: Select the heading and edit Text Content. Keep the change small enough that you can recognise it immediately.

items.title: Preview the flow

sections.title: A small example you can read end to end

blocks.text: The following .ui example adapts the counter shown in the repository README. It keeps its logic inline so the relationship between a variable, a button and the rendered text is visible in one place. Use the source editor for the example rather than assuming every construct is visually rewritable.

blocks.code:
<logic>
  let count = 0

  function increment() {
    count = count + 1
  }
</logic>

<App theme="dark">
  <Stack direction="vertical" gap="md" padding="lg">
    <Heading level={1}>My first SoftN app</Heading>
    <Text>Count: {count}</Text>
    <Button variant="primary" @click={increment}>Increment</Button>
  </Stack>
</App>
blocks.caption: Illustrative counter adapted from the documented .ui syntax. This edition has not run it inside SoftN.

blocks.text: The count variable stores the current value. The Text expression displays it. The Button’s @click binding calls increment, which updates the variable. SoftN connects script state back to the interface.

Add a reset function that sets count to zero, then bind a second Button to that function. This is a useful first exercise because it uses the same state and event pattern without introducing persistence or networking.

blocks.caption: Add this function inside the existing logic block.

blocks.code: <Button @click={reset}>Reset</Button>
blocks.caption: Place this button beside the existing Increment button inside the Stack.

blocks.text: A variable in this example is live app state. It is not a durable database record. Closing and reopening the app is a separate test from rerendering its interface. Use the XDB guide when you are ready to keep records.

blocks.text: You have completed the important first loop when you can explain which source change produced which visible behaviour, and reproduce it from the exported bundle.

sections.title: Customise a copy, not a mystery

blocks.text: Choose an example because it demonstrates a specific need: a form flow, responsive layout, audio feedback or scene interaction. Keep an unchanged copy and make one change at a time so you know which part caused a new behaviour.

Do not assume that an example’s backend or permissions are included with its client source. Read its requirements and confirm the host-specific setup. Connected workspace examples are particularly important to distinguish from standalone local apps.

Change one Fieldnotes label, add one optional field to the data model and test the resulting flow in a fresh exported copy. That gives you a practical lesson in UI, records, seeds and portability without introducing an unrelated service.

pages.title: SoftN Builder
pages.summary: Shape the interface, inspect source, model data and preview a portable app in one editable workspace.

seo.title: SoftN Builder | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn SoftN Builder for visual app editing, source changes, collection schemas, responsive previews and exporting portable .softn apps.

blocks.text: Builder is the place to shape an app you can inspect and keep editing. The documented workspace combines a visual canvas, properties, source editing, schema editing and previews for different screen sizes.
You can start a project, reopen a .softn bundle or use Fieldnotes as a working example. A visual change is a change to an editable app, not a commitment to abandoning its source.

items.title: Open or create
items.text: Begin with a known bundle or a blank project. Keep a copy before making a large structural change.

items.title: Edit the interface
items.text: Select a component and change a property such as the heading’s Text Content. Preview the actual interaction, not only the canvas layout.

items.title: Inspect behaviour
items.text: Use Code view to understand the logic behind actions. Keep related changes small enough to test independently.

items.title: Review the data
items.text: Use Data view for collection structure and the seeds the app will carry.

items.title: Preview and export
items.text: Check the sizes you support, export the bundle and reopen that exported copy.

sections.title: Visual editing and Code view work together

blocks.text: Not every source construct is safe for a canvas to rewrite. The README explicitly describes keeping such files editable in Code view. Treat that as protection for the source, not a reason to simplify a working app until the canvas accepts it.

Use visual editing where the tool exposes a clear control. Use source editing for complex behaviour and source structures that do not round-trip safely through the canvas. After either route, run the same user flow again.

sections.title: Preview data and exported seeds are different jobs

blocks.text: Fieldnotes demonstrates that Builder preview has its own test records while Data view exposes the seeds carried by the bundle. An app that looks populated in preview may still need careful seed preparation for a first-time user.

blocks.title: Test a fresh start
blocks.text: Reopen the exported bundle in a clean test context and check empty lists, first records and initial settings. This is more informative than repeatedly testing only your populated workspace.

sections.title: Preview is a check, not an automatic redesign

blocks.text: The preview runs the app at desktop, tablet and mobile sizes. Responsive behaviour still depends on the layout you authored. Check forms, navigation, long text and tables at the narrowest size you plan to support.
For a first project, stop when one core flow is reliable: create a record, display it, change it and reopen the export. Add visual polish after that path is dependable.

sections.title: Turn a brief into an editable starting point

blocks.text: Studio is SoftN’s AI-assisted creation workflow. The README describes configured OpenAI, Anthropic or custom providers. You bring the provider configuration, describe the app and review the generated result.
AI generation is one way to create an app, not a requirement for using SoftN. Existing bundles and manually written source can be opened and edited without asking an AI provider to generate anything.

A useful brief names the people using the app, the records they manage, the screens they need and what each important button should do. Specify what stays local and which operations, if any, need a backend.

blocks.code:
Create a local task planner for one person.

Screens: task list and a small summary dashboard.
Each task needs a title and completion status.
Let me add a task, mark it complete and filter the list.
Use local records. Do not add login, AI calls or a backend.
Make empty states clear and keep the phone layout readable.
blocks.caption: An example brief, not a special Studio command language.

blocks.text: Start with one complete loop instead of asking for every feature at once. It is easier to review a working task flow than a large collection of unfinished screens.

items.title: Read the source and permissions
items.text: Check that the result matches the brief and does not request capabilities the app does not need.

items.title: Exercise the main interaction
items.text: Create, change and display a record. Check invalid input and the empty state.

items.title: Try narrow layouts
items.text: Check labels, controls and navigation on a phone-sized preview.

items.title: Export and reopen

blocks.text: Using an external AI provider can involve that provider’s credentials, service limits and charges. Review the configuration and the provider’s applicable terms before sending content. Do not place private access tokens in app source or a downloadable bundle.

blocks.title: Generation is not validation
blocks.text: Generated logic and UI still need review. A convincing explanation is not proof that a function exists, an export is complete or a permission is granted.
Use Builder and Code view to refine the result. The useful outcome is an app whose behaviour you understand and whose source you can change, not a single prompt you can never reproduce.
For a connected app, describe the client and backend responsibilities separately. A generated interface is not, by itself, a deployed authentication system or private API.

pages.title: SoftN Runtime
pages.summary: Open bundles, switch between running apps and understand what the browser library does and does not keep.

seo.title: SoftN Runtime | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn SoftN Runtime: open .softn bundles, browse apps, use the saved browser library, switch running apps and understand host support.

sections.title: The place to use an app

blocks.text: Runtime opens and runs .softn bundles. The web experience can open bundles, explore directory apps and return to a library saved in the current browser. The project also has a Tauri desktop loader.
Creation tools help you change an app; Runtime helps you use it. The same bundle can be reopened in an editor when you decide to customise its interface or behaviour.

sections.title: Home is not the same as Close

blocks.text: The documented web workspace keeps apps running when you return to its home view. That lets you browse or open another app without discarding an unfinished form. Use Home to switch between apps and Close to stop the current app.

This is a lifecycle distinction worth testing in your own app. Navigating within a running workspace, closing an app and reopening a saved bundle can involve different state and persistence behaviour.

Apps you open are kept in the current browser’s library, with offline readiness shown for saved apps. That does not make browser storage an account-wide cloud backup. Another device, another browser profile or cleared site storage can have different contents.

blocks.title: Check offline readiness before relying on it
blocks.text: A saved app may still use network services or remote resources. Test the actual workflow without a connection and keep a separate copy of important exports.

sections.title: The host decides what the app can reach

blocks.text: A capability needs support and permission from the host. A browser can also require its own consent for camera or microphone access. A desktop build may support native storage or other integrations that are unavailable in an ordinary browser.
The bundle’s manifest name is not a universal storage account. The general bundle loader, single-app deployments and FormLogic integration each have identity rules that affect records and grants.

items: Open the exported bundle, not only its editor preview.
Exercise the main flow and return Home without losing unfinished input.
Close and reopen, then check which state is intended to persist.
Review permission requests and test denial as well as approval.
Confirm the host and browser you actually plan to support.

blocks.text: When something differs between preview and Runtime, first identify whether the difference is UI state, data seeds, persistent records, host capability support or deployment configuration.

pages.title: The .softn app format
pages.summary: What a bundle contains, what an export leaves behind, and how to think about source, seeds and permissions.

seo.title: The .softn app format | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn the .softn file format: a portable ZIP-based app bundle containing editable UI, client logic, metadata, data seeds, assets and permissions.

blocks.text: A .softn file is a ZIP-based app bundle. It packages the editable client material that SoftN needs to load an app. This makes it a useful handoff between creation tools and runtimes: you can export an app, reopen it and change its source.

The format is not a promise that every external dependency lives inside the archive. A remote service, an AI provider or a private server database still has its own deployment and access requirements.

blocks.code:
my-app.softn
├── manifest.json
├── permission.json
├── ui/
├── logic/
├── xdb/
└── assets/
blocks.caption: Typical client layout documented by the project. Exact files depend on the app.

items.description: App metadata, configuration and its entry point. Export from Builder or use a current example rather than guessing required fields.
The capabilities the app requests from its host. Declaring a capability is not the same as receiving a grant.
The interface and reusable UI source.
The client behaviour, normally JavaScript-compatible .logic files.
Optional collection seeds carried with the app.
The images, styles and other distributable assets the app needs.

sections.title: Seeds are not automatically a backup of live records

blocks.text: Seed records provide starting content for a new app instance. The records someone creates while running an app belong to that host’s storage and identity rules. Do not assume that exporting a project also exports every user’s live database.

Builder’s preview uses test records. Use its Data view to review the seeds you intend to distribute, then test a fresh runtime instance. This prevents a demo from appearing complete only because it is using your existing local data.

sections.title: Separate client downloads from private deployment

blocks.text: The repository also describes server-side .logic resources for server hosts. Those resources are not executed by the browser. A backend deployment must decide how to keep private scripts, credentials and SQLite databases on the server.

blocks.title: Assume a recipient can inspect the bundle
blocks.text: Anything shipped in a downloadable client archive should be material you intend to share. Do not use an editable client bundle to hide a service secret or a private database.

sections.title: Identity and compatibility belong to the host too

blocks.text: The general bundle loader uses a digest to isolate bundles. Configured single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own deployment identity. An app name by itself does not grant access to another app’s records or permission grants.
Test a bundle on the host you intend to use. A successful export confirms packaging, not browser microphone consent, backend authorisation or support for every optional capability.

pages.title: The SoftN UI language
pages.summary: Read component tags, expressions, bindings and control flow without needing to learn every component at once.

seo.title: The SoftN UI language | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn SoftN .ui syntax: components, expression props, event handlers, two-way binding, conditional rendering and list rendering.

blocks.text: A .ui file describes the interface using component tags, properties and expressions. SoftN parses the source and renders the result through React. The app source is SoftN syntax, not a React component that you must rewrite as JSX.

The README shows inline logic inside a logic block, along with separate .logic files in bundles. Use a current exported example to follow the project structure for external files instead of guessing an import convention.

blocks.code:
<Button variant="primary" size="md">Save</Button>
<Text>{message}</Text>
<Text color={isDark ? "white" : "black"}>{message}</Text>
blocks.caption: Examples of literal properties and brace-delimited expressions.

blocks.text: Quoted values are literal strings. Braces contain expressions whose values come from the app’s state and context. Start with simple expressions and move complicated decisions into named logic functions.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Enter your name" />
<Button @click={save}>Save</Button>
blocks.caption: The username state and save function must be defined by the app.

blocks.text: The :bind form connects the input to state. The @click form binds an action to a function. Ordinary template DOM events are not passed through as raw browser event objects; see the state and events guide before relying on event.target or browser methods.

blocks.code:
#if (isLoggedIn)
  <Text>Welcome back</Text>
#else
  <Text>Please sign in</Text>
#end

#each (task in tasks)
  <Text>{task.title}</Text>
#empty
  <Text>No tasks yet</Text>
#end
blocks.caption: Control-flow syntax using app-owned state. Here tasks is an ordinary array of objects with a title field, not a claim about XDB record shape.

blocks.text: An empty branch makes the first-run experience explicit. It is often more helpful than a blank area that leaves the user wondering whether the app has loaded.

Use layout components for structure, display components for readable content and form components for actions and input. Reusable app components can keep repeated sections consistent, but their exact file wiring should follow a current bundle example.

blocks.title: Keep the first screen readable
blocks.text: A heading, a short explanation, one input and one action can be enough to test a complete interaction before you add navigation and dashboards.

pages.title: JavaScript logic with ZIPP
pages.summary: Write app behaviour in .logic while understanding the difference between language support and host APIs.

seo.title: JavaScript logic with ZIPP | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN .logic and ZIPP: JavaScript app behaviour, the Rust and WebAssembly engine, host bridges and browser runtime boundaries.

blocks.text: SoftN’s .logic files use JavaScript and run in the ZIPP engine, which is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. The README documents classes, async/await, destructuring, closures and other familiar JavaScript features.

The engine executes the language. SoftN supplies the app integration: state, rendering and explicitly exposed host APIs. Knowing JavaScript does not imply that every browser global, Node.js module or npm package is available inside a script.

blocks.caption: A small app-logic pattern from the documented database bridge. The host must provide the collection and database integration.

blocks.text: The initialisation function loads records. The action creates a record and refreshes the state used by the interface. This explicit pattern is easier to inspect than burying data changes inside a display expression.

sections.title: The engine and the host are separate layers

blocks.text: ZIPP’s browser build is an interpreter inside WebAssembly. The upstream project’s native JIT tiers are not the execution path used by that browser artifact. Native benchmark results should not be presented as SoftN browser performance.

The host decides what a script can call. The SoftN README describes bridges such as db and the softn APIs, with gated capabilities controlled by declarations and host grants. A bridge object’s existence is not a reason to assume unrestricted access.

blocks.title: Browser JavaScript is still outside the guest
blocks.text: Treat .logic as guest code running in its provided environment, not as a script tag with ambient access to the whole page.

sections.title: Use the bundled engine as your compatibility reference

blocks.text: The retrieved README identifies the browser engine as ZIPP v0.0.18 and points to SOURCE.json for artifact provenance. It also describes a local combined JavaScript and experimental Python build. The exact bundled artifact matters more than an upstream release headline.
For ordinary SoftN development, use the checked-in runtime. Rebuilding the engine is a separate maintenance task with its own Rust and WebAssembly tooling.

sections.title: Learn the boundaries before adding integrations

blocks.text: Start with app state and XDB. When you add networking, media, GPU work or backend actions, use the relevant host-facing guide and test both allowed and denied behaviour. A working JavaScript expression proves less than a complete user flow.

pages.title: State, events and app lifecycle
pages.summary: Connect user actions to state, understand event data, and distinguish a running screen from durable records.

seo.title: State, events and app lifecycle | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn SoftN state and events: action handlers, two-way binding, lifecycle checks, window input and the difference between state and saved records.

sections.title: State connects behaviour to the interface

blocks.text: SoftN’s documented state flow synchronises script globals with the React-side component state around script calls. Expressions in the interface read that state so changes made by an action can appear in the UI.

For a small app, keep important state obvious: a current filter, a form field, the records shown in a list or the selected item. Use named actions to change it. This makes it easier to trace a click from the template to the function and back to the screen.

sections.title: Template events are not raw DOM events

blocks.text: The README states that an ordinary template binding such as @click={fn} calls the handler without passing the raw DOM event; the event is reduced to null. Do not assume a template handler can call event.preventDefault or read event.target.

Callbacks with meaningful component data are a different case. The documented examples include DPad @press and Slider @change passing their data through. Check the contract for the component you use rather than treating every callback identically.

blocks.code:
<Input :bind={username} placeholder="Name" />
<Button @click={save}>Save</Button>
blocks.caption: Read the bound username state inside save rather than expecting a DOM input event.

blocks.text: The README describes window.addEventListener as the route for scripts that need plain-data keyboard or pointer events. The host supplies selected fields such as clientX, clientY, key and targetTag rather than handing the guest an unrestricted browser object.
Box and Button forward pointerdown, pointerup, pointercancel and pointerleave, supporting controls that react while held. Account for cancellation and leaving the control, not only the initial press.

blocks.code: softn.input.captureKeys(["ArrowUp", " ", "F1"])
blocks.caption: Documented key-capture API. The host protects text fields, Ctrl combinations and the system modifier.

blocks.text: Use key capture only for keys your app genuinely needs. A game should not make it unnecessarily hard to type into its own settings form or use familiar browser shortcuts.

rows: Does the interface update after an action?
Does unfinished input survive returning Home and switching apps?
Does intended data survive closing and reopening the app?
blocks.caption: These are separate acceptance checks, not interchangeable definitions of persistence.

blocks.text: Use XDB for record-oriented storage. A counter variable or selected tab is not automatically a database record. Decide which state should restart and which state should be restored.

sections.title: Trace one interaction at a time

items.title: Check the binding
items.text: Confirm the template refers to the function and state you intended.

items.title: Check the function
items.text: Reduce it to one state change before adding database or network work.

items.title: Check the host boundary
items.text: Permission, capability support and backend availability can fail independently of the UI.

items.title: Check the lifecycle
items.text: Reproduce whether the issue appears after a rerender, app switch, close or fresh open.

pages.title: SoftN component guide
pages.summary: Find a sensible starting component for layouts, forms, data, charts, media, animation and richer apps.

seo.title: SoftN component guide | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Explore SoftN components for layouts, forms, tables, dashboards, charts, media, animation, editors and Three.js scenes.

sections.title: Choose a component by the job it does

blocks.text: The README organises the built-in library into layout, form, display, feedback, data, navigation, utility, chart, animation, editor, 3D and smart components. Start with the role you need rather than a list of every property.

This is a component discovery guide, not a complete property reference. The names below are documented exports in the retrieved README; use a current example or implementation reference when you need exact property types and callback values.

rows: App, Box, Stack, Grid, Card, Container, Layout, Header, Content, Section
Text, Heading, Badge, Tag, Progress, Spinner, Image, Icon
Button, Input, TextArea, Select, Checkbox, Radio, Switch, Form, Slider
Alert, Modal, Toast, Drawer, Popover, EmptyState
blocks.caption: A starting selection from the documented component library.

blocks.text: Choose the simplest component that matches the interaction. A small settings screen may need only a Stack, Heading, Input and Button. More components do not necessarily make the workflow clearer.

rows: List, ListItem, Table, DataGrid, TreeView, Pagination
LineChart, BarChart, PieChart, AreaChart, RadarChart, GaugeChart
blocks.caption: Smart components offer data-driven configuration; ordinary components give you more direct presentation control.

blocks.text: Use a table when someone needs to inspect individual records. Use a chart for a question about a pattern or comparison. A chart is most useful when its labels, units and empty state make that question understandable.

The documented library also includes PixelGrid, PixelCanvas, QRCode, QRReader, Camera, Microphone, AudioStream and DPad; animation components such as AnimatedBox, AnimatedNumber, Sprite and TileMap; editors such as CodeEditor, MarkdownEditor and RichTextEditor; and Scene3D for Three.js scenes.

Their presence in the library does not remove browser constraints or host permissions. Media input and advanced host integrations should be checked in the actual deployment, not only in a component catalogue.

sections.title: A practical way to learn a component

items.title: Find a working example
items.text: Start with a bundle that already uses the component for the same kind of task.

items.title: Change one property
items.text: Keep the behaviour understandable while you learn its configuration.

items.title: Test the callback
items.text: Confirm what data an event supplies before writing logic around it.

items.title: Test the awkward case
items.text: Try an empty collection, long label, narrow screen or denied permission.

pages.title: Forms, tables and dashboards
pages.summary: Build a useful record workflow before adding extra screens, summaries and visual polish.

seo.title: Forms, tables and dashboards | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Build SoftN forms, tables and dashboards with XDB, SmartForm, SmartGrid and clear record workflows, validation and empty states.

blocks.text: A record-oriented app usually needs a small loop: enter information, save it, show the result and update it later. Build that loop before adding several dashboards. It makes the relationship between the interface, logic and data easier to test.
SoftN documents both ordinary form and data components and smart components that use a collection-oriented configuration. Choose the route that makes your app’s behaviour easiest to explain.

blocks.code:
<SmartForm
  collection="clients"
  fields="name:text:required, email:email:required, phone:text"
  submitText="Add Client"
/>
blocks.caption: A small configuration adapted from the README. The surrounding app must supply the collection and data context.

blocks.text: The example identifies the collection and fields, including required name and email inputs. Treat validation at the UI as help for the user, not a substitute for checks on a private backend that accepts submitted data.
Decide what happens after a save: clear the form, keep values for a similar next record, show a confirmation or return to a list. Test that the user can tell whether the operation succeeded.

blocks.code:
<SmartGrid
  collection="clients"
  columns="name, email, phone, visits"
  searchable sortable pageable
/>
blocks.caption: A read-oriented configuration adapted from the README. Add editing only after defining and testing the intended update flow.

blocks.text: Choose columns for the task, not merely because the fields exist. Long text and too many columns can make a phone layout difficult. A list or card layout may be a better small-screen view.

sections.title: Add summaries that answer a question

blocks.text: SmartStats, chart components and ordinary display components can turn records into a dashboard. Give each summary a clear meaning: open tasks, visits during a period or records needing follow-up. Label the time window and units where they matter.
Compute summaries from the same intended records as the list. A dashboard and table that disagree may be using different filters, stale state or preview data instead of the live collection.

items: Start with no records and confirm the next action is clear.
Submit incomplete or invalid values and check the explanation.
Create a record and confirm it appears in the view.
Update a record and verify totals and filters still agree.
Reopen the app and check the intended persistence.
Check phone-sized layouts and keyboard access.

blocks.text: When the flow needs shared authenticated records, add a backend deliberately. Local XDB storage and server authorisation solve different problems.

pages.title: Local app data with XDB
pages.summary: Understand collections, record operations, seeds, app identity and optional synchronization.

seo.title: Local app data with XDB | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn XDB in SoftN: local collections, synchronous record operations, bundle seeds, app-scoped storage and host-dependent synchronization.

blocks.text: XDB is SoftN’s documented local-first data layer. It provides app-scoped records and a database bridge to app logic. The README describes synchronous CRUD operations backed by an in-memory cache, with persistence and native storage depending on the host.

Think of a collection as records of one kind, such as clients or tasks. Think separately about the collection’s schema, its starting seed records and the live records a person creates while using the app.

blocks.caption: CRUD call shapes shown in the README, with example data changed. Do not run the final delete when you intend to keep the example record.

blocks.text: Create and query name a collection. Update and delete use a record identifier in the documented examples. Do not invent a SQL query language or assume that a record’s field shape matches a plain application object without checking the current API.
For a reactive screen, make it clear when the state shown by the UI is refreshed. The README’s small logic example queries records at initialisation and queries again after creating a record.

Builder exposes collection structure and seed data. Use schemas to make field intent clear, and ship only seeds that are appropriate for recipients. Do not distribute a real customer dataset merely because it made a convincing local demo.

blocks.title: Preview is not the exported database
blocks.text: Builder preview has its own test records. Review the seeds in Data view and test a fresh app instance before assuming the export contains the intended starting data.

sections.title: App identity is not just a display name

blocks.text: The general loader isolates bundles by digest, while configured single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own identity. A display name alone is not an authority to read another app’s data.
Treat upgrades and moving between hosts as data-lifecycle decisions. Before changing an identity or deployment, test which records remain available and keep a recovery copy appropriate to that host.

blocks.code: await db.startSync('my-room-name')
blocks.caption: The README’s synchronization entry point. The host must support and permit sync.

blocks.text: A room name is not an authentication or privacy policy. Decide who may participate, how access is controlled and what the host actually provides before using synchronization for sensitive or multi-user records.
Local persistence, peer-to-peer sync and a private server database are not interchangeable features. Choose the one that matches the app’s ownership, sharing and recovery needs.

pages.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts
pages.summary: Keep an app readable, portable and testable across sizes without relying on your own browser cache.

seo.title: Assets, themes and responsive layouts | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Manage SoftN assets, light and dark themes, and responsive layouts. Test exported bundles, narrow screens and fresh app instances.

sections.title: Keep distributable assets with the app

blocks.text: A typical bundle includes an assets directory for images, styles and other app resources. The README describes asset() for template asset resolution and the audio API resolving bundle paths in the same way.

A local file that exists only on your development machine is not automatically part of the exported app. Reopen the exported bundle in a fresh context to catch missing resources that your current preview or browser cache may hide.

blocks.code: <Image src={asset("assets/cover.png")} />
blocks.caption: An illustrative use of the documented asset helper with an Image component. Include the referenced file in the app.

sections.title: Design for the theme you support

blocks.text: The README’s introductory app uses an App theme property and demonstrates Fieldnotes in light and dark presentations. It also describes switching the runtime theme without clearing unfinished input.

Test your own colours in each supported theme. A hard-coded text colour that works on one background can become unreadable on another. Use meaning, labels and shape as well as colour to communicate status.

sections.title: A preview size is a test case

blocks.text: Builder previews desktop, tablet and phone sizes, but responsive behaviour is still part of the authored layout. Switching preview size does not automatically redesign an overflowing table or a navigation bar with too many items.

items: Check the narrowest screen you intend to support.
Try long headings, validation messages and realistic record values.
Keep important controls reachable without horizontal scrolling.
Check how charts and tables behave when their container shrinks.
Test the actual interaction after a theme or viewport change.

blocks.text: A remote image, font, audio file or model makes the app depend on a network service even when its records are local. Decide whether the asset should be bundled, fetched when needed or treated as optional.

For an app that must work offline, test after the host reports the saved app ready, then disable the connection and exercise the real workflow. The word local-first does not automatically package a remote resource.

items.title: Export
items.text: Build the bundle you actually intend to distribute.

items.title: Open fresh
items.text: Avoid relying only on an existing populated preview.

items.title: Check assets
items.text: Look for missing images, fonts, models or audio.

items.title: Check layout
items.text: Use a phone-sized viewport and each supported theme.

items.title: Check ownership
items.text: Include only assets you have permission to distribute.

pages.title: How SoftN, ZIPP and XDB fit together
pages.summary: A readable map of the interface, guest logic, data and hosting responsibilities.

seo.title: How SoftN, ZIPP and XDB fit together | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN architecture: .ui rendering through React, .logic in the ZIPP WebAssembly engine, XDB records and optional backend hosts.

sections.title: A small map of the platform

blocks.text: SoftN connects an editable UI language, application behaviour and records. Its architecture is easier to understand when you keep the renderer, the script engine, the database and the host as separate responsibilities.

blocks.code:
Editable .softn client bundle
  |
  +-- .ui source --> SoftN parser / renderer --> React interface
  |
  +-- .logic ----> ZIPP bytecode VM ----------> app behaviour
  |
  +-- XDB seeds and assets

Host integration connects behaviour to app-scoped records
and explicitly supported, granted capabilities.

Optional private backend
  authenticated actions --> server logic / server database
blocks.caption: Conceptual responsibility map. A backend is separate from a public client download.

blocks.text: The README describes a lexer, parser and renderer turning .ui source into React elements through a component registry. Component properties and template expressions connect the visible interface to the app’s state.
The developer works with SoftN’s source format. React is part of the host’s rendering implementation, not a requirement that every app author maintain a separate React project.
ZIPP compiles guest source to register bytecode and executes it. In the browser, the published WebAssembly build uses its interpreter rather than the upstream native JIT tiers.

SoftN synchronises script globals and UI-side state around script calls and supplies host bridges. This is why a button handler can update a variable and change a rendered expression without receiving unrestricted access to the browser’s entire environment.

XDB supplies app-scoped local records. Bundle seeds can provide starting content, while the host controls persistence and identity. Optional synchronization and native storage depend on what the host supports and allows.
A private SQLite database on a server is a different resource with different access rules. A client can request named backend operations without receiving a copy of that database or its credentials.

Builder, Studio and Runtime can work with the same editable bundle, while a browser, desktop loader or configured website provides the execution environment. FormLogic is an optional connected host with its own authenticated backend path.

blocks.title: A shared engine is not shared authority
blocks.text: The README describes hosts sharing verified engine bytes while each worker or app keeps its own instance, memory and permissions. Reusing an artifact does not mean sharing a running VM or granting access between apps.

sections.title: Read the layer you are changing

pages.title: Audio, microphone and media
pages.summary: Add sound deliberately, understand autoplay, and distinguish playback from access to a person’s microphone or camera.

seo.title: Audio, microphone and media | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Use audio and media in SoftN. Learn documented sound playback, browser autoplay behaviour, microphone and camera permissions and testing.

blocks.text: The README documents softn.audio for playing sound from .logic. Asset paths are resolved inside the bundle. Playback is different from microphone capture: playing a bundled sound does not read microphone data.

blocks.caption: Documented playback calls. Declare themeHandle in your app state and include both audio files.

blocks.text: The documented setVolume operation scales current and subsequent playback. The runtime stops the audio an app started when that app closes.

Browsers can refuse playback before the user interacts with the page. SoftN’s documented one-shot result reports played: false and blocked: true in that situation. A looped soundtrack is deferred until a click or keystroke.
Design the first screen so sound is optional rather than the only explanation of what is happening. A visible Start action is easier to understand than an app that depends on immediate audio.

blocks.title: Test on a fresh page
blocks.text: A browser that has already received your clicks is not a useful test of the first-visit autoplay path.

sections.title: Microphone and camera are different permissions

blocks.text: The documented component library includes Camera, Microphone and AudioStream. Capture requires host support and the relevant permissions, and the browser may also ask the person for consent.
The audio playback API is not permission-gated in the same way as microphone capture. Do not broaden an app’s requested capabilities merely to play a bundled sound effect.

blocks.title: Ask only when the feature needs it
blocks.text: Explain what capture is for and provide a useful denied-permission state. Do not silently upload captured material or embed private service credentials in the client.

items: Try a fresh session before any interaction.
Try permission denial and a device without the requested input.
Check that playback and capture stop at the intended point.
Check volume, mute behaviour and visible feedback.
Try the browser and host you plan to support, not only the development preview.

blocks.text: Exact capture callbacks and advanced speech APIs are outside this introductory guide. Use the project’s current media and local-speech references for the version you deploy.

pages.title: 3D apps and games with SoftN
pages.summary: Combine a readable interface with scenes, controls, animation and sound without confusing rendering with engine execution.

seo.title: 3D apps and games with SoftN | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Explore 3D apps and games in SoftN with Scene3D, Three.js, animation, pixel components, input and sound, plus browser performance checks.

sections.title: An app can be more than a form

blocks.text: SoftN’s documented component library includes Scene3D backed by Three.js, along with animation, sprite, tile and pixel-oriented components. Those building blocks make interactive scenes and games possible within the same editable app format.

Keep the game’s responsibilities clear. The scene displays the world; controls capture player intent; .logic updates the app’s state; and the host provides supported capabilities. A settings panel or task list can use ordinary UI components around the scene.

sections.title: Choose the presentation the interaction needs

rows: DPad and supported pointer or keyboard input
Text, overlays and the softn.audio playback API
blocks.caption: Select a small set of components, then test one playable interaction.

blocks.text: The README names GLTF, OBJ, FBX and STL in its Scene3D description. Follow a working example for the exact model-loading and scene configuration contract rather than guessing component properties.

The state and events guide explains the difference between template callbacks and the host’s plain-data keyboard and pointer events. For a held control, account for release, cancellation and leaving the control area.
Plan what happens when a player opens settings, switches apps or closes the game. A running workspace, an in-memory game state and a saved game are different lifetimes.

ZIPP’s browser artifact is interpreter-only; native JIT performance is not a prediction of game performance in a SoftN browser host. Rendering, scene complexity, asset loading, script work and host-boundary traffic can all affect responsiveness.
Start with a small scene and one interaction. Measure frame time, startup time and memory while adding content, rather than trying to diagnose a fully populated world all at once.

blocks.title: Rendering and compute are separate
blocks.text: A Three.js scene is not proof that the app can call every ZIPP GPU-compute API. Host support, integration and permission still determine access.

sections.title: Check playability, not just a screenshot

items: Make the first action obvious and provide a restart path.
Keep important text and controls readable on a small viewport.
Test missing audio permission or blocked autoplay where relevant.
Use bundled assets or document the required network resources.
Test the exported bundle for longer than a single successful frame.

blocks.text: For your first game, one reliable loop with a clear outcome is a better test of the platform than a large map with unfinished controls.

pages.title: Permissions and sandboxing
pages.summary: Understand requested capabilities, host grants, browser consent and the limits of an editable client bundle.

seo.title: Permissions and sandboxing | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN permissions and sandboxing: permission.json, host grants, network allowlists, browser consent and private client-server boundaries.

sections.title: Three questions before an app uses a capability

blocks.text: A useful way to reason about a host operation is to ask: does the app declare it, does this host support and grant it, and does the surrounding browser or service allow it? Those checks can fail independently.

The README describes gated capabilities including networking, camera, microphone, filesystem, AI, GPU, synchronization, server storage and host acceleration. A bundle without the relevant declarations can still run ordinary UI and logic, but cannot assume access to those host operations.

blocks.caption: The network permission shape shown in the README. example.com is a placeholder, not a service supplied by SoftN.

blocks.text: A declaration requests a capability. It does not authenticate to that API, grant server-side access or prove that a destination is appropriate. Use the smallest set of destinations and operations the app needs.
Treat permission.json as part of the app’s public explanation. Someone opening the bundle should be able to understand why a task planner or media app needs each requested capability.

sections.title: The host boundary is part of the design

blocks.text: The browser uses the ZIPP WebAssembly engine for guest logic and SoftN exposes the supported integration points. ZIPP’s published documentation describes default-deny host calls and distinguishes installing a bridge from granting authority.

Sandboxing is an implementation boundary, not a promise that every app or host is risk-free. Host code, app data handling, resource limits and private backend authorisation still need appropriate testing.

blocks.title: No client-side hiding place for secrets
blocks.text: A .softn bundle is editable, inspectable source. Keep service credentials and private server databases in a deployment designed to keep them on the server.

A friendly app name is a label, not a storage credential. General bundle loading uses digest-based isolation; configured single-app and FormLogic hosts use their own deployment identity. Test what happens to data and grants when publishing an update.

items.title: Remove an unneeded capability
items.text: Confirm that the app’s core local flow still works.

items.title: Deny a needed capability
items.text: Show a clear explanation and a way to continue or stop safely.

items.title: Try an unsupported host
items.text: Distinguish not supported from not granted and from a service error.

items.title: Review the download
items.text: Confirm that private material did not enter the client archive.

sections.title: What this guide does not certify

blocks.text: These pages describe the documented capability model. They do not certify a deployment’s security or assert that any particular host configuration is safe for sensitive records. Review the actual version, host policy and backend before making that decision.

pages.title: Offline use, local data and app identity
pages.summary: Know what your browser keeps, what an export carries and what needs a separate backup or server.

seo.title: Offline use, local data and app identity | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand offline SoftN apps, browser libraries, local records, bundle seeds, host identity and the limits of local-first persistence.

sections.title: Local-first describes a data approach, not every dependency

blocks.text: SoftN’s README describes app-scoped XDB records and a browser library for opened apps. Saved apps show offline readiness. Those features help a local workflow, but they do not make a remote API or externally hosted asset available without a connection.
Test the actual app flow offline, not only whether its first screen opens. A form might be local while its submit action or background image still depends on a server.

sections.title: Keep four kinds of state separate

rows: The client source, configuration, seeds and distributable assets
What is currently happening in a live app, such as unfinished input
Data kept by the app’s storage integration and identity
Server-side records governed by that deployment’s access rules
blocks.caption: Exporting or closing one of these does not automatically transfer or preserve the others.

blocks.text: Builder preview data adds another testing context. Use Data view to inspect the seeds you plan to distribute, and check a fresh Runtime instance to see the recipient’s starting experience.

sections.title: Treat the browser library as this browser’s library

blocks.text: The documented web library keeps apps opened in that browser. It is not a universal account-wide library merely because the app has a name. A different profile or host can have a different library and storage context.

Keep a separate exported copy of important app source. For important live records, use the backup or export facilities provided by the chosen host and confirm that you can restore them. Do not assume the project export button is a complete record backup.

sections.title: An update can involve identity decisions

blocks.text: The general loader uses bundle digests for isolation. Configured single-app and FormLogic hosts provide their own deployment identity. Before shipping an update, test whether the host treats it as the same app for records and grants.

blocks.title: Test upgrades before replacing a working app
blocks.text: Use a non-production copy with representative records. Check loading, identity, schema changes and the recovery path.

items.title: Prepare the app
items.text: Open the intended bundle and check the host’s offline-readiness indication.

items.title: Create a test record
items.text: Use a disposable record whose presence you can recognise.

items.title: Disable the connection
items.text: Exercise the real workflow, including assets and any submit action.

items.title: Close and reopen
items.text: Check which local data survives and which network operations need to wait.

items.title: Restore the connection
items.text: Confirm the app handles returning online without confusing duplicate or failed actions.

pages.title: JavaScript, Python and compatibility
pages.summary: Use JavaScript for documented SoftN app logic and treat the experimental Python frontend as a separate integration concern.

seo.title: JavaScript, Python and compatibility | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Understand SoftN language support: JavaScript .logic, the bundled ZIPP engine, experimental Python and why host integration matters.

sections.title: JavaScript remains the documented app path

blocks.text: The retrieved SoftN README says existing .logic screens continue to use JavaScript. It identifies the checked-in browser engine as ZIPP v0.0.18, built locally with JavaScript and experimental Python support.

Those statements describe two different layers: languages present in an engine artifact, and languages wired into an app’s normal UI, state and lifecycle. Do not assume that including a frontend automatically turns a .logic screen into a Python screen.

ZIPP’s published Python guide describes a Python 3 frontend that parses source and lowers it to the same register bytecode VM. It is an implementation of Python semantics on that engine, not an embedded CPython process or a general pip environment.

The guide lists supported language features and documented gaps. Its Torch-related work is explicitly an experimental API subset, not native PyTorch or CUDA. Refer to that guide for the current compatibility scope instead of advertising unrestricted package compatibility.

blocks.title: Experimental means test the exact workflow
blocks.text: A successful standalone Python example is not proof of SoftN UI binding, database integration or support for a particular third-party package.

sections.title: Engine entry points are not automatically app syntax

blocks.text: The published ZIPP browser API includes initSource(source, language) and a Python-project entry point. Those are engine-embedding APIs for hosts. This documentation does not invent a SoftN manifest language flag, Python file binding syntax or Python UI lifecycle that has not been verified.

Before adopting Python in a SoftN app, consult the repository’s language-support guide and check the actual host integration. For the ordinary app workflow described here, use JavaScript-compatible .logic.

rows: Does the language parse and run?
The engine frontend and its documented language support
The libraries and bridges exposed by this artifact and host
UI state, events, permissions, assets, data and lifecycle on the target host
blocks.caption: Language conformance, package compatibility and application compatibility are different checks.

blocks.text: Avoid treating an upstream JavaScript conformance result as proof of Node.js API compatibility, browser DOM access or Python package support. Each belongs to a different contract.

pages.title: Hosting and deploying SoftN apps
pages.summary: Choose between opening a bundle, publishing an app, hosting one website or connecting a private backend.

seo.title: Hosting and deploying SoftN apps | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Compare SoftN deployment routes: browser and desktop bundles, the app directory, single-app websites, private backends and FormLogic hosting.

sections.title: Choose the host before configuring everything

blocks.text: SoftN separates the editable client app from the environment that runs it. The README documents browser and desktop runtimes, app-directory publishing, single-app websites, private PHP serving, server logic with SQLite and FormLogic integration.

These are different deployment paths, not a checklist every app must complete. A local planner may need only a bundle and Runtime. An authenticated shared dashboard needs an explicit backend and access policy.

rows: Capabilities and storage depend on the host
Publishing a discoverable app with a player page
Review client downloads, metadata and publication requirements
One app on its own website
Configure app identity, paths and the intended public files
Serving client material from a private deployment archive
This does not make code delivered to a browser secret
Keep credentials and database access server-side
The host owns authentication and named backend access
blocks.caption: Deployment routes described in the project README.

blocks.text: A downloadable .softn bundle contains material a recipient can inspect. A private server deployment contains resources that should remain on the server. Do not expect a client export to package, secure and migrate a live backend automatically.
If the app has no server requirement, keep it simple. If it does, name the operations the client needs and decide which identity and permissions the server uses to authorise each operation.

items.title: Test the exported client
items.text: Run the bundle outside the editor preview and check assets, seeds and layout.

items.title: Choose stable identity rules
items.text: Test records and grants across an update using the host’s documented identity model.

items.title: Separate private resources
items.text: Review the client archive and public web directory for unintended material.

items.title: Test capabilities
items.text: Check approved, denied and unsupported cases on the actual host.

items.title: Test recovery
items.text: Keep a known-working release and a tested approach for recovering important records.

sections.title: Use the project’s documented build commands

blocks.text: The root package scripts include build:site, build:single and packaging commands for single-app and private PHP routes. This guide does not guess their flags, archive layouts or required environment variables: follow the linked deployment guides for the version you are building.

blocks.code:

sections.title: A website focused on one app

blocks.text: The README describes an unbranded single-app runtime for deploying a SoftN app on its own website. This is the route for making one app the experience, rather than asking visitors to begin in a general-purpose app library.
The app remains a SoftN client. Its editable interface and logic are still distinct from any private service it calls. A custom domain does not change which material is delivered to the browser.

blocks.text: The README distinguishes configured single-app identity from the digest-based identity used by the general bundle loader. That matters when an updated bundle should still see the intended records and permission state.

Test an update using disposable records before changing a live deployment. Confirm whether the new version opens the same data context and how schema or seed changes affect an existing user. Do not treat the visible app name as a guaranteed migration key.

sections.title: Check the served app, not only the build

blocks.text: After staging the output, open the actual deployed path and verify every needed asset. Missing bundles, incorrect base paths, stale caches and mismatched engine files can look like application failures.

For WebAssembly hosts, the engine glue and binary belong to the same artifact. Avoid deploying one without its matching counterpart. Check the actual bundled SoftN engine rather than substituting an upstream artifact based only on its version label.

A single-app site can be the client for private backend operations, but credentials and a server database should remain in the server deployment. Delivering UI to a browser does not make its source confidential.

sections.title: When an app needs a server

blocks.text: A local app does not necessarily need a backend. A server becomes useful when records are shared under authentication, a private service credential is needed, or an operation must be controlled outside the editable client.

The README documents server-side .logic and SQLite deployment routes, including a Rust private backend and PHP backend packaging. It also describes FormLogic as a separate connected hosting path. Do not assume those hosts use identical configuration.

blocks.text: A server resource packaged for deployment is not a script the browser should execute. The client should know what operation to request, not carry a private database or service secret.

sections.title: Private serving is not secret client code

blocks.text: The README also links a private PHP serving route that serves an app from a private archive. Keeping an original archive outside a public directory can be useful deployment hygiene, but material sent to a browser remains inspectable.

blocks.title: Review the public output
blocks.text: Before deploying, inspect both the downloadable client bundle and the public web directory. Keep private server scripts, credentials and databases out of client downloads.

Start with a few named operations whose inputs, outputs and authorisation rules are understandable. For example, a planner might need a create-task operation and a list-visible-tasks operation, with the server deciding what the authenticated person can access.

Those names are design examples, not built-in SoftN APIs. The actual request wiring depends on the host. Use the relevant host documentation rather than inventing a shared protocol across every deployment route.

pages.title: SoftN and FormLogic
pages.summary: Understand the difference between exporting an editable starter and running an authenticated connected workspace.

seo.title: SoftN and FormLogic | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Learn SoftN and FormLogic integration: editable starter exports, local XDB, connected iframe apps and named backend actions owned by the host.

blocks.text: SoftN supplies the editable app and runtime. The retrieved README describes FormLogic as the hosted workspace for forms, records, backend actions and app databases. Connecting them does not erase the client-server boundary.

There are two documented integration paths: converting a supported form into a local-first starter, and running an app as a connected workspace under a host. Choose the path before assuming what an export contains.

The canonical adapter converts supported FormLogic form schemas into editable .softn bundles. The README says the starter uses local XDB data with sync set to false and excludes responses, credentials and access grants.

That makes a starter a starting app structure, not a copy of a live account or an automatic connection to the original form’s private data. Inspect the result, customise it and test its local record workflow.

blocks.title: An export is not an access grant
blocks.text: Downloading the client does not transfer permission to a live FormLogic backend.

The connected host renders app source in an isolated iframe. Client logic calls named backend actions through softn.backend.call, while the parent host owns authentication and applies the selected app’s permissions.

This guide identifies the documented API family, not an unverified argument signature. Use the current connected-host source and workspace examples to confirm action names, input shapes and error handling for the version you deploy.

The README points to editable FormLogic and Aokie workspace examples. Aokie’s workspace brings calls, appointments, messages, follow-ups and transcripts into an interface, while the communication services remain part of the host integration.
A workspace example demonstrates a client experience. It is not evidence that downloading that bundle also provisions telephony, authenticated records or every external service it displays.

sections.title: Keep server resources on the hosting platform

blocks.text: For custom server .logic and SQLite, configure those resources on the hosting platform and expose the operations the client needs. Keep private scripts, credentials and databases server-side.

The README also describes FormLogic reusing verified ZIPP engine bytes while each worker or hosted app retains its own instance, memory and permissions. Shared engine delivery is not a shared app-data context.

pages.title: Troubleshooting SoftN apps
pages.summary: Identify whether a problem belongs to the interface, logic, data, permissions, assets or host before changing several layers.

seo.title: Troubleshooting SoftN apps | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Troubleshoot SoftN app loading, state updates, records, permissions, audio, offline use, responsive layouts and backend connections.

sections.title: Find the layer before changing the app

blocks.text: A blank screen, missing record or failed request can come from different layers. Begin by identifying whether the problem is in the exported bundle, UI source, logic, local records, permission state, asset delivery or host configuration.
Reproduce with the smallest known app or interaction. Keep the original export so you can compare a failing change with a working copy.

items.title: Check the artifact
items.text: Open the exact exported .softn file you plan to share, not only the editor project.

items.title: Check the host
items.text: Confirm the target supports the bundle and required capabilities.

items.title: Check delivery
items.text: For a website, confirm the intended bundle, assets and matching engine files are being served.

items.title: Check the error context
items.text: Record the host, browser, app version and visible error without exposing credentials or private records.

sections.title: The button works but the screen does not change

blocks.text: Check that the template binds the intended function, that the function changes the intended state and that the displayed expression reads that state. Reduce the action to a simple state change before adding database or network work.
Do not expect a raw DOM event in an ordinary @click template handler. Use bound state or the documented callback data for that component.

sections.title: The records look missing or different

blocks.text: Distinguish Builder preview test records, exported seeds and live Runtime records. Then check the host identity. A general bundle digest, a configured single-app identity and a FormLogic deployment are not automatically the same storage context.
Do not clear storage as a first step when it contains important records. Preserve a recoverable copy through the host’s supported facilities before testing destructive changes.

Check declaration, host support, the host’s grant and any browser or service consent separately. A network allowlist does not authenticate to a server; a browser microphone approval does not prove that the app declared the capability correctly.

sections.title: Sound does not play on first load

blocks.text: The documented playback API handles blocked autoplay. A one-shot can report that playback was blocked, while a looped track waits for a user interaction. Try a clear Start action and check that the bundled path exists.

sections.title: It works in preview but not elsewhere

blocks.text: For layout differences, test the exact viewport and theme rather than assuming responsive preview rewrites the app. For offline differences, check remote assets and backend calls as well as the host’s offline-readiness status.
For a connected app, confirm that the expected backend and authentication context exist in the target host. A client export does not carry a live backend session.

items: What you expected and what happened instead.
The smallest steps needed to reproduce it.
The app version, host, browser and operating environment.
Whether it fails in preview, the exported bundle, or both.
A minimal sanitised bundle or source excerpt when it is appropriate to share.

blocks.text: Keep credentials, private records and personal capture data out of public issue reports.

pages.title: SoftN frequently asked questions
pages.summary: Straight answers about the app format, accounts, AI, local data, hosting, JavaScript and experimental Python.

seo.title: SoftN frequently asked questions | SoftN Docs
seo.description: Answers to common SoftN questions about .softn files, AI accounts, Builder, Runtime, local data, hosting, FormLogic and language support.

blocks.text: SoftN is an open-source UI language, visual builder and runtime for editable web and desktop apps. A .softn bundle brings the client interface, logic, data seeds and assets together so the app can be reopened and customised.

It is a ZIP-based portable app bundle. Typical contents include manifest.json, permission.json, UI source, client logic, optional XDB seeds and distributable assets. Export from Builder or follow a current example instead of guessing the manifest structure.

sections.title: Do I need an AI account?

blocks.text: Not to try Fieldnotes or work directly with app source. Studio’s AI-assisted creation path uses your configured provider. That provider can have its own credentials, service limits and charges.

sections.title: Do I have to write code?

blocks.text: Builder offers visual editing, schema work and preview. Source remains available for behaviour and structures that need direct editing. It is more accurate to describe an editable visual-and-code workflow than to promise that every possible app needs no code.

XDB provides app-scoped local records through the host. Persistence, native storage and synchronization depend on that host. A connected backend can keep separate server-owned records. Bundle seeds and a user’s live records are not the same thing.

The browser library shows offline readiness for saved apps. A particular app may still depend on remote assets or backend operations, so test its real workflow without a connection before relying on offline use.
It uses JavaScript, but it runs inside ZIPP with the APIs the host exposes. Do not assume unrestricted DOM access, Node.js APIs or automatic support for arbitrary npm packages.

The retrieved README says existing .logic screens continue to use JavaScript while the bundled engine includes experimental Python support. Language support inside an artifact is not the same as verified Python UI and data integration. Follow the dedicated language-support guide.

sections.title: Can I put an app on its own domain?

blocks.text: Yes. The project documents a dedicated single-app runtime. Use its current configuration guide, check deployment identity and keep any private backend resources separate from the public client.
No. It is an optional connected hosting route. The README distinguishes local-first starter exports from authenticated hosted workspaces that call named backend actions.

sections.title: Can I hide an API key in the bundle?

blocks.text: Treat every client bundle as inspectable. Keep private service credentials on a server and expose only the authorised operations the client needs. A custom domain or private source archive does not make material sent to a browser secret.

The retrieved repository declares Apache-2.0 licensing. When redistributing a complete app or deployment, also review its included assets, dependencies and any applicable notices rather than assuming every third-party resource has identical terms.

sections.title: Are these docs a complete API specification?

blocks.text: These pages provide friendly workflow and concept coverage based on the accessible documentation. They are not an exhaustive property reference or a completed source audit. Detailed host configuration and experimental integration should be checked against the exact version you deploy.
